messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Arjun

Arjun was thirty-six when he first came to therapy, though the lines around his eyes and the careful way he held his shoulders made him seem older. He worked as an accountant for a mid-sized firm in suburban New Jersey, the kind of role that suited his methodical mind and his need for control—spreadsheets did not surprise you, did not raise their voices, did not suddenly turn violent. But control had become his prison, and the very habits that once protected him were now suffocating him.

The trauma lived in his childhood, in a house in Gujarat before his family immigrated when he was seven. He could not quite assemble the memory into a coherent narrative, though fragments surfaced unbidden: his mother's cry from the kitchen, his father's shadow looming across the hallway, the sound of breaking glass that seemed to splinter something inside Arjun's own body. He remembered hiding behind the sofa, his small hands pressed against his ears, and the terrible knowledge that he could do nothing to stop what was happening. He was too small, too powerless, too young. By the time his parents divorced years later—a separation that came as relief but also as confirmation that he had been right to be afraid—Arjun had internalized a conviction that would shadow him for decades: the people who had caused this suffering had never truly been held accountable. His father had simply left, remarried, built a new life. The violence had been absorbed into the family's silence, wrapped in shame and never spoken of again. And Arjun, left with the wreckage of his mother's grief and his own fractured sense of safety, had come to believe that bad things happened to people like him, that he was fundamentally unable to prevent disaster.

This helplessness had metastasized into a broader despair. He used to be happy—he remembered that about himself, though the memory felt like something from someone else's life. His mother had photographs of him as a boy, grinning at birthday parties, but those photographs belonged to a different Arjun, one who had not yet learned that the world was a place where fathers hurt mothers and children were powerless to stop it. Now, at thirty-six, he was always miserable. The happiness had drained away so gradually he could not pinpoint when it left, but it was gone, replaced by a low, persistent dread that colored everything. This despair fed his sense of threat. Because he believed he could not protect himself, because he felt certain that consequences never came for the people who hurt others, his body remained in a state of constant vigilance. He was always scanning, always alert, muscles perpetually tensed as though bracing for the next blow. His nervous system had learned that danger was real and that he was defenseless against it.

The memories themselves were both the trigger and the consequence of this state. When something in his surroundings—a raised voice in the office, the sound of shattering dishes when a colleague dropped a mug in the break room, even the particular quality of late afternoon light through a window—pulled him back to that moment behind the sofa, the terror returned with full force. It was not a memory he could think about calmly; it was a reliving, a physiological rupture. His heart would race, his hands would shake, and for a few seconds he would not know where he was. These intrusions were wordless—he could not describe them to anyone, could barely articulate them to himself. But once they seized him, they reinforced everything he believed about himself and the world. The terror confirmed that danger was real and ever-present. The fact that he could not control when these memories arrived, that they ambushed him without warning, deepened his conviction that he was helpless, that bad things happened to him without mercy or logic.

This vicious spiral had cost him his marriage. His ex-wife had tried for years to reach him, to understand why he flinched at loud noises, why he could not be spontaneous, why he seemed to be disappearing into himself. But Arjun could not explain it—the memories were too fragmented, the fear too overwhelming to articulate. His hypervigilance, which had once felt like necessary protection, had become a wall between them. He monitored her every mood, her every tone, waiting for the moment when safety would shatter. She had finally left, and though part of him understood that his own behavior had driven her away, another part of him had simply confirmed what he already knew: that he could not prevent loss, that he was incapable of keeping people safe or holding onto happiness.

He came to therapy now because the spiral had tightened to the point where he could barely function. His work had suffered; he made mistakes he would never have made before, his concentration fractured by the constant state of alert. He sat in the waiting room with his hands clasped tightly in his lap, afraid that if he let himself relax for even a moment, something catastrophic would happen. What he wanted most was to feel safe again, to believe that he could have some say in what happened to him. What he feared most was that this was simply who he was now—broken, helpless, forever waiting for the next disaster.
